titre: The present perfect: a first look
intro: The present perfect (I have worked, she has seen) connects the past and the present. It is one of the most difficult tenses for learners, so this lesson takes it step by step.
objectifs: Form the present perfect with have / has + past participle, in all forms.
Know the most common irregular past participles.
Use the present perfect for life experience and for a past action with a result now.
Choose between the present perfect and the past simple: is there a finished past time?

texte: The present perfect uses the helper verb have (has for he / she / it) + the past participle. Short forms: I've, you've, he's / she's / it's, we've, they've; negative haven't / hasn't.
Be careful: “he's” can mean “he is” or “he has”. The next word tells you: “he's tired” (is) / “he's finished” (has + past participle).

lignes: We haven't eaten. He hasn't called.
Yes, I have. / No, she hasn't.
Has he arrived? — No, he hasn't.

texte: For regular verbs, the past participle is the same as the past simple: base + -ed (worked, played, studied, stopped).
For irregular verbs, it is the third column of the list (go – went – gone). Some verbs have the same past simple and past participle; others don't, so learn both.
Use the present perfect to say what you have done (or not) in your life until now, without saying when. The experience matters, not the time.
The words “ever” and “never” are very common with this use: you will study them in detail in the next lesson (52).
exemples: She has worked in three countries.

sections.titre: Use 2: a past action with a result now
texte: We also use it for a recent action when we can see the result now. The present situation is what matters.
Often a present sentence could say the same thing: “I've lost my keys” = I don't have my keys now.
exemples: I've lost my keys. I can't open the door.
He's broken his leg, so he can't play.

texte: The golden rule: when you say (or think of) a finished past time — yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child — use the past simple, never the present perfect.
In conversation, we often start with the present perfect (the experience), then change to the past simple for the details (when, where, how).
exemples: I've met the new manager. I met her this morning.
Experience, then the detail in the past simple.
Have you ever been to Brussels? — Yes, I went there last summer.
Question in the present perfect, answer with a time in the past simple.

texte: The verb go has two possible participles in the present perfect, with different meanings. “Has been to” = went there and came back (experience). “Has gone to” = went there and is still there (not here now).

formule: have / has + past participle (worked, seen, gone, been…)
prononciation: In speech, have and has are contracted and very short: I've /aɪv/, we've /wiːv/, she's /ʃiːz/. Listen for the small /v/ or /z/ sound.
In a question, “have” is weak: Have you seen…? /həv juː ˈsiːn/. In a short answer, it is strong: Yes, I HAVE /hæv/.
erreurs: After have: past participle (gone / been), not the past simple.
eat → ate → eaten: you need the participle.
When asks about the time: past simple.
He has gone to Paris twice.
He has been to Paris twice.
The helper is always have, never be, even with verbs of movement.

dialogue.contexte: In Brussels, Clémence is interviewing Olivier for a job in a travel agency.
lignes: So, Olivier, have you worked in tourism before?
Yes, I have. I worked in a hotel in Liège for two years.
Short answer, then a finished period: past simple.
Great. Which countries have you visited?
I've been to Morocco, Cameroon and Canada. I went to Canada last year.
been to (experience); last year → past simple.
Have you ever organised a group trip?
ever = at any time in your life.
No, I haven't, but I've helped my manager with several trips.
OK. And have you read our job description?
Result now: do you know it?
Yes, I have. I've prepared some ideas for your website, too.

mots: She has a lot of experience.
knowledge or skill you get from doing something
before now, or sooner than expected
more than two but not many
in the last few days or weeks
to damage something so it is in pieces (break – broke – broken)

exercices.consigne: Complete with have, has, haven't or hasn't.
items: They ___ moved to a new flat.

exercices.consigne: Put the verb in the present perfect or the past simple.
items: She ___ (start) her new job last Monday.
Where's Amina? — She's ___ to the bank. She'll be back soon.
I've ___ to Ghent twice. It's beautiful.
My parents aren't here. They've ___ to Yaoundé for a week.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I have finished it two hours ago.
I finished it two hours ago.
He have bought a new car.
He has bought a new car.

exercices.consigne: Write five sentences about your experiences: three in the present perfect, then two in the past simple with details.
items: I've lived in two countries. I've learned to drive and I've visited many cities in Africa. I visited Accra in 2023 and I loved it. I learned to drive when I was 19.

a_retenir: Present perfect = have / has + past participle (worked, seen, gone, been, done).
Life experience with no time: I've been to Canada.
Past action with a result now: I've lost my keys.
Finished past time (yesterday, in 2020, ago, When…?) = past simple, never present perfect.
been to = went and came back; gone to = went and is still there.
